title: Atomic Structure
description: Protons, neutrons, electrons — and what they actually mean

concepts.title: The Three Subatomic Particles
concepts.contentHtml:
An atom has three building blocks:

Protons — positively charged, in the nucleus.
Neutrons — no charge, also in the nucleus.
Electrons — negatively charged, orbiting in shells around the nucleus.

Protons and neutrons have nearly identical mass; electrons are about 1,800 times lighter. Almost all the mass of an atom is in the tiny nucleus.

Most of an atom is empty space — if a hydrogen atom's nucleus were a marble, the electron would be roughly a kilometer away.

concepts.title: Atomic Number and Mass Number
concepts.contentHtml:
The atomic number is the number of protons. It defines what element the atom is — 1 proton = hydrogen, 6 protons = carbon, 79 = gold. Change the proton count and you change the element.

The mass number is protons + neutrons.

Atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are isotopes. Carbon-12 (6 neutrons) and carbon-14 (8 neutrons) are both carbon, but C-14 is radioactive and used for radiocarbon dating of once-living material up to about 50,000 years old.

concepts.title: Electron Shells
concepts.contentHtml:
Electrons occupy shells around the nucleus. Each shell holds a maximum number: the first holds 2, the second holds 8, the third holds 8 (initially).

The outermost shell is what determines chemistry. Atoms 'want' a full outer shell — typically 8 electrons (the octet rule).

Noble gases (helium, neon, argon) already have full outer shells, so they barely react. Reactive elements (sodium, chlorine) are one electron away from a full shell, so they grab or shed electrons eagerly.

title: Chemical Bonds
description: How atoms join to form molecules

concepts.title: Ionic Bonds
concepts.contentHtml:
An ionic bond forms when one atom donates electrons to another. The donor becomes a positive ion (cation); the receiver becomes negative (anion). Opposite charges attract — that's the bond.

Classic example: sodium chloride (table salt). Sodium has 1 outer electron and gives it up; chlorine has 7 and grabs the spare. The resulting Na⁺ and Cl⁻ stick together.

Ionic compounds form crystal lattices, dissolve well in water, and conduct electricity when dissolved.

concepts.title: Covalent Bonds
concepts.contentHtml:
A covalent bond is when two atoms share electrons rather than transferring them. Both atoms get effectively full outer shells through cooperation.

Water (H₂O) is covalent: oxygen shares one electron with each of two hydrogens, and they share back.

Covalent bonds can be single, double, or triple, depending on how many electron pairs are shared. They're typically stronger than ionic bonds and form discrete molecules rather than crystal lattices.

Most of life's molecules — DNA, proteins, sugars — are held together covalently.

concepts.title: Metallic Bonds
concepts.contentHtml:
In a metallic bond, atoms pool their outer electrons into a shared 'sea' that flows freely between positively charged metal ions.

This explains why metals are:

— Conductive (free electrons carry current and heat)
— Malleable (atoms can slide past each other without breaking the bond)
— Shiny (free electrons reflect light)

The 'electron sea' model is why a copper wire conducts and a salt crystal doesn't, despite both being held together by electric attraction.

title: The Periodic Table
description: Why elements are arranged the way they are

concepts.title: Groups and Periods
concepts.contentHtml:
The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number, but the genius is in the layout.

Periods are the rows. Each new period adds an electron shell.

Groups are the columns. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer-shell electrons, so they behave chemically similarly.

Group 1 (alkali metals): all have 1 outer electron — all violently reactive with water. Group 18 (noble gases): all have full outer shells — all unreactive. The table reveals chemistry by geography.

concepts.title: Periodic Trends
concepts.contentHtml:
Properties change predictably across the table:

Atomic radius generally increases down a group (more shells) and decreases across a period (more protons pulling tighter).

Electronegativity (how strongly an atom attracts electrons) increases up and to the right. Fluorine (top right of nonmetals) is the most electronegative element.

Ionization energy (energy to remove an electron) follows the same pattern as electronegativity — small, tightly held atoms hold onto their electrons hardest.

concepts.title: Mendeleev's Genius
concepts.contentHtml:
Dmitri Mendeleev built the first useful periodic table in 1869 — before electrons were even discovered.

He arranged elements by atomic weight and noticed that properties recurred periodically. Where his pattern broke, he predicted missing elements — and even their properties (gallium, germanium) — years before they were discovered.

This kind of predictive power separates scientific theories from mere classifications. The periodic table didn't just organize known chemistry — it told us what to look for. The modern version is sorted by atomic number rather than weight, but the basic insight stands.

title: Chemical Reactions
description: Reactants in, products out — and what's conserved

concepts.title: Balancing Equations
concepts.contentHtml:
A chemical reaction rearranges atoms — none are created or destroyed (law of conservation of mass). So a balanced equation must have the same atom counts on both sides.

Hydrogen + oxygen → water:

H₂ + O₂ → H₂O ❌ (oxygen unbalanced)
2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O ✅

Coefficients (2 H₂, 2 H₂O) tell you how many molecules participate. Subscripts (the 2 in H₂O) tell you the molecule's structure.

concepts.title: Reaction Types
concepts.contentHtml:
Most chemical reactions fall into a few families:

— Synthesis: A + B → AB (combining)
— Decomposition: AB → A + B (breaking apart)
— Single replacement: A + BC → AC + B
— Double replacement: AB + CD → AD + CB
— Combustion: hydrocarbon + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + energy

Recognizing the type helps you predict products. Combustion reactions, in particular, power most of human civilization.

concepts.title: Endothermic vs Exothermic
concepts.contentHtml:
Reactions either release energy or absorb it.

Exothermic: products have less energy than reactants — the difference is released as heat. Combustion, freezing, neutralization. Touch the container — it gets warmer.

Endothermic: products have more energy than reactants — the difference is absorbed from the surroundings. Cold packs, photosynthesis, melting. The container gets colder.

Whether a reaction proceeds spontaneously depends not just on energy but also entropy (disorder) — captured by Gibbs free energy.

title: Acids, Bases & pH
description: The chemistry behind sourness, soap, and biology

concepts.title: Acids and Bases
concepts.contentHtml:
A simple definition (Brønsted–Lowry):

An acid donates a proton (H⁺).
A base accepts a proton.

HCl in water → H⁺ + Cl⁻. The HCl gave up its proton — it's an acid.

NaOH in water → Na⁺ + OH⁻. The OH⁻ readily grabs a proton — it's a base.

Acids taste sour (lemons, vinegar); bases taste bitter and feel slippery (soap, baking soda). But don't taste them in a lab.

concepts.title: The pH Scale
concepts.contentHtml:
pH measures how acidic or basic a solution is. It runs from 0 (most acidic) to 14 (most basic), with 7 being neutral.

The scale is logarithmic: each unit is 10× the H⁺ concentration. pH 4 has 1000× more H⁺ than pH 7.

Examples:

— Stomach acid: ~2
— Lemon juice: ~2.5
— Pure water: 7
— Baking soda: ~9
— Drain cleaner: ~13

Blood pH must stay between 7.35 and 7.45 — even small drifts are life-threatening.

concepts.title: Neutralization and Buffers
concepts.contentHtml:
When an acid meets a base, they neutralize:

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O

The acid's H⁺ combines with the base's OH⁻ to form water; the leftover ions form a salt.

This is why antacids relieve heartburn (base neutralizes stomach acid) and why baking soda neutralizes vinegar.

A buffer is a special mixture that resists pH change — biological systems are full of them. Your blood's bicarbonate buffer keeps pH stable despite the constant acid/base load of metabolism.

title: Quantum Atomic Models
description: From Bohr to orbitals — how electrons really live

concepts.title: Why Bohr's Model Fails
concepts.contentHtml:
Bohr's 1913 model — electrons in fixed circular orbits — explained hydrogen's emission spectrum but failed for any atom with more than one electron. It also can't explain why electron orbits don't simply radiate away their energy by classical electrodynamics.

The problem is that electrons aren't point particles in orbits at all. They are quantum waves — distributions of probability — described by the Schrödinger equation.

concepts.title: Atomic Orbitals
concepts.contentHtml:
Solving Schrödinger's equation for hydrogen gives discrete energy levels and wavefunctions called orbitals: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3d, etc. Each orbital is a 3D probability distribution.

Three quantum numbers index orbitals: n (energy/size), l (shape: s, p, d, f...), m_l (orientation in space). A fourth, m_s, gives spin (±½). The Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons share all four.

concepts.title: Multi-Electron Atoms
concepts.contentHtml:
For atoms beyond hydrogen, electron-electron repulsion rules out exact analytical solutions. The aufbau ('building up') principle fills orbitals in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d... — note that 4s comes before 3d.

Hund's rule: electrons fill degenerate orbitals (e.g., the three 2p orbitals) singly first, with parallel spins, before pairing.

The periodic table's structure (s-, p-, d-, f-block) reflects exactly this filling pattern. Periodicity is a direct consequence of quantum mechanics.

title: Periodic Trends in Depth
description: Why the table works the way it does

concepts.title: Atomic Radius and Effective Nuclear Charge
concepts.contentHtml:
Going across a period, atomic radius decreases (more protons pull electrons in). Going down a group, radius increases (more shells).

The effective nuclear charge Z_eff is the net positive charge an outer electron actually feels — nuclear charge minus screening from inner electrons. Z_eff increases across a period; that's why ionization energies and electronegativities also rise.

concepts.title: Ionization Energy & Electron Affinity
concepts.contentHtml:
Ionization energy (IE): energy to remove an electron. Sudden jumps reveal closed-shell stability — losing an electron from a noble-gas core is enormously unfavorable.

Electron affinity (EA): the energy change when an electron is added (negative means energy is released). Halogens have very negative EA (eager); noble gases have positive EA (refuse).

The two trends correlate: high IE plus high EA defines an electronegative element. Cesium has the lowest IE; fluorine has both high IE and high EA.

concepts.title: Lanthanide Contraction & d-Block Anomalies
concepts.contentHtml:
The 4f orbitals fill across the lanthanides (Ce-Lu). 4f electrons screen poorly, so Z_eff felt by 5d/6s electrons rises sharply, contracting them.

Consequence: 5d transition metals (Hf-Hg) end up nearly the same size as 4d counterparts. This is why 2nd and 3rd transition rows are chemically so similar, why Au, Pt, Hg are dense, and why gold is yellow (relativistic narrowing of the 5d-6s gap into the visible).

Periodic trends repay patient study — they encode real physics, not just bookkeeping.

concepts.title: Oxidation and Reduction
concepts.contentHtml:
Oxidation: loss of electrons. Reduction: gain of electrons. The two always happen together — one species' electrons go to another.

Mnemonic: OIL RIG. Oxidation Is Loss; Reduction Is Gain.

Bookkeep electrons by assigning oxidation states — the charge an atom would have if all bonds were ionic. Useful even when the bonds aren't really ionic.

concepts.title: Standard Reduction Potentials
concepts.contentHtml:
Tendency to be reduced is measured by the standard reduction potential E°, in volts. F₂ + 2e⁻ → 2F⁻ gives E° = +2.87 V (loves electrons); Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li has E° = −3.04 V (hates them).

For a full redox reaction, ΔE° = E°(cathode, reduced) − E°(anode, oxidized). Positive ΔE° means spontaneous; coupled with ΔG° = -nFE°.

This is the basis of every battery and every corrosion process.

concepts.title: Redox in the Wild
concepts.contentHtml:
Combustion: organic compounds get oxidized to CO₂ and H₂O. Photosynthesis is the reverse, driven by sunlight. Cellular respiration recovers the energy.

Rust: Fe → Fe²⁺ at the anode (later oxidized further to Fe³⁺); O₂ + H₂O → OH⁻ at the cathode. Galvanizing protects iron by attaching a more readily oxidized metal (zinc) — the zinc corrodes first, sacrificially.

Bleach (sodium hypochlorite) oxidizes pigments. Vitamin C and other antioxidants intercept biological oxidation chains. Even diet intersects with electrochemistry.
